intro: A gently accumulating string phrase gives the slow movement its pulse. Listen for that same repeated-note material becoming insistent and chromatic in the middle, then recovering its quieter shape.
question: When the opening returns, does its steady pulse sound reassuring or newly vulnerable?

sections.label: Exposition · repeated notes and replies
sections.mNote: E♭ major opening; contrasting ideas move towards B♭

sections.label: Recapitulation · the opening reconsidered
sections.mNote: The principal material returns in the tonic

cues.title: A theme assembled
cues.text: The opening grows from repeated notes in the violas. Successively higher string parts take up the figure; the tune emerges through imitation rather than arriving as a single finished melody.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, II, bars 1–8, PDF p. 19; report 0:00–0:30 has a quiet opening and a gradual rise in relative level. The cue describes the opening passage, not individual entry times.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three symphonies in weeks
cues.text: Mozart enters his last three symphonies in his own catalogue during the summer of 1788. This G minor work stands between the E♭ major No. 39 and the C major “Jupiter”.
cues.evidence: Marianne Williams Tobias, Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note, Symphony No. 40 (2015), https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.

cues.title: Small notes matter
cues.text: Through this gentler movement, listen for the quick little figures between the longer notes. They can be decorative in one phrase and become the material of an argument in another.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, II, bars 20–32, PDF pp. 20–21; report 1:00–1:20 is relatively quiet and suggests the B♭ region. No particular instrumental entry is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The quiet surface breaks
cues.text: In this stretch the short figures gather weight. The orchestra’s stronger statements interrupt the delicate exchange; an Andante can sustain conflict without changing its underlying pace.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 25–36, PDF pp. 21–22, contrasts wind figures with full-ensemble forte. The report has boundaries at 1:38 and 1:50, then relative level rises from −21.0 dB at 1:45 to −8.3 dB at 2:00. This is a passage estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two orchestral versions
cues.text: Mozart later adds clarinets and rewrites the oboe parts. The source of this performance does not identify which version is used, so the guide does not assign its wind colours to a particular version.
cues.evidence: IMSLP work page and Breitkopf score footnote; Commons and upstream Musopen metadata do not name the version. See this recording’s dossier.

cues.title: A close becomes a beginning
cues.text: The exposition settles towards its close, but its little repeated-note figure remains available. The next span takes that familiar pulse into more unsettled harmonic territory.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 44–57, PDF p. 23: exposition closes at bar 52 and development begins at 53. Report has a strong boundary at 3:06 and a renewed rise around 3:10–3:15. The join is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chromatic pressure
cues.text: The middle passage makes the semiquaver figures more insistent. Wind chords and moving strings repeatedly press against one another; the music sounds more crowded although the metre has not changed.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 58–65, PDF p. 24; report boundaries 3:24, 3:34 and 3:48, with relatively high level across 3:25–3:45. Instrumental roles come from the score, not the feature analysis.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A public-domain project
cues.text: This performance comes from Musopen’s Kickstarter collection. Commons credits “Musopen Symphony”, while the upstream file names the Czech National Symphony Orchestra; the guide preserves that unresolved attribution rather than supplying a conductor.
cues.evidence: Commons file page and Internet Archive MusopenCollectionAsFlac metadata, track 110; see dossier.

cues.title: The opening finds home
cues.text: The returning material restores E♭ major and the recognisable repeated-note pulse. Listen for continuity in the rhythm even after the middle section has made the same small figures sound more urgent.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 74 onward, PDF pp. 25–26; report settles around E♭ at 4:25–4:50 after the stronger central span. The recapitulation marker at 4:24 is proportional and provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Replies across the orchestra
cues.text: Listen across a whole phrase rather than following only the highest line. Short replies pass between strings and winds, while the repeated notes keep the movement connected beneath them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf II, recapitulation, PDF pp. 26–28; report 5:06 boundary and lower relative level around 5:10–5:20 support a quieter passage. This is a listening strategy, not an entry map.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Letters asking for help
cues.text: Letters from this period ask Mozart’s fellow Freemason Michael Puchberg for financial help. They document a difficult household economy; they do not establish that this movement represents a particular private sorrow.
cues.evidence: Marianne Williams Tobias, Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note, Symphony No. 40 (2015), https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. Composer biography, Vienna and final-symphony context.

cues.title: Force followed by space
cues.text: The contrast between firm ensemble statements and quieter replies persists near the end. Notice how a sudden reduction in sound leaves the underlying pulse exposed instead of simply stopping the movement.
cues.evidence: Report 6:02 boundary, level around −9.5 dB at 6:20, then −28.2 dB at 6:30; Breitkopf II, closing recapitulation, PDF pp. 28–29. The cue covers the contrast, not a precise attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cadence without a sprint
cues.text: The final phrases still work with the movement’s measured pulse. Follow the bass towards the close and notice how the quick upper figures can settle without turning into a fast finale.
cues.evidence: Report shows a renewed high-level span at 7:00–7:10, quieter closing windows at 7:15–7:30, and sound ending by 7:36; Breitkopf II, final page 29.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The pulse changes its surroundings
transitions.how: A B♭-major cadence closes the exposition. The development restarts the repeated-note idea in the strings, then brings in stronger wind chords and chromatic semiquaver movement. The link is motivic rather than a new tempo: the same small figure now works in an unstable harmonic setting.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 51–58, PDF pp. 23–24; report boundary 3:06 and the rise around 3:10–3:15. Bar-to-time placement is provisional.

transitions.title: The fragments recover their shape
transitions.how: The busy central texture thins, leaving short wind replies above the strings. The opening repeated-note idea then re-forms in E♭ major. The return is recognisable through texture and rhythm as well as key: separate imitative lines again build a continuous phrase.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf II, bars 66–76, PDF p. 25; report quieter 4:00–4:20 span followed by E♭-centred windows from 4:25. The marker does not claim an aligned downbeat.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: II. Andante; PDF pp. 19–29, especially bars 1–8, 25–36, 53–65 and 74 onward. Both versions are printed together. Clarinets and version-specific oboe detail are not inferred from this recording. Timings are provisional passage estimates, not aligned entrances.

timeline.note: Opening passage: the viola figure rises through the string parts; not simultaneous entrances.
Horns support the string-led opening paragraph; winds otherwise rest in the early score.
Short wind figures answer the strings in the exposition; version-specific oboe detail is withheld.
Development passage: repeated-note strings alternate with stronger ensemble statements.
Wind chords and semiquaver figures share the more forceful middle paragraph.
The opening string pattern returns; the marker covers a passage, not an entry.
Closing paragraph alternates full sonority with quieter string-led replies.

facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
